edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SCIENCE & TECH + SPORT
edition.deck: A French school protest movement grows amid clashes; a major Hollywood merger closes; and Denmark investigates a breach exposing records of 8.8 million people.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments across international, UK and Danish news, with space for science, public services and environmental impact. Related reports on the same events are grouped rather than treated as separate stories.

content.headline: French school protests spread as concerns mount over police force
content.shortHeadline: French school protests spread amid police violence concerns
content.standfirst: Tens of thousands marched as students protested overcrowded classes, teacher shortages and run-down schools. Rights groups and demonstrators have also raised concerns over police tactics and serious injuries.

image.caption: Protesters march in Marseille during demonstrations over conditions in French schools.

sources.originalTitle: Schools blockaded as tens of thousands of protesters take to streets in France
How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?
‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policing

segments.body: Nearly 90,000 students, staff and parents joined marches across France on Tuesday, according to the interior ministry, while hundreds of high schools were blockaded. Students are demanding action on long school days, absent teachers and deteriorating buildings; Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has instructed ministers to address their complaints.

segments.title: Injuries and investigations
segments.body: The protests have also brought clashes with police. Government figures cited by the Guardian report at least 715 officers and 215 teenagers injured, and 6,100 arrests since demonstrations began. Amnesty International has criticised what it calls disproportionate force; the interior minister says 10 internal investigations into alleged police brutality are under way.

perspectives.body: Students interviewed in Paris described feeling that police force was excessive and that it overshadowed their calls for better-funded, more equal schools. The report also records the government’s account of arrests and injuries.

content.headline: Paramount completes $110bn takeover of Warner Bros Discovery
content.shortHeadline: Paramount completes $110bn Warner Bros takeover
content.standfirst: The deal brings major film studios, streaming services and newsrooms under one company, after legal challenges and concerns about competition, jobs and editorial independence.

image.caption: Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery are joining under the Skydance name.

sources.originalTitle: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger
From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you
Budkrig og 737 milliarder senere er kæmpe mediefusion gennemført

segments.body: Paramount Skydance has completed its $110bn acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, bringing companies including HBO, CBS, CNN, Nickelodeon and DC Studios under the Skydance Corporation name. Paramount says the combined business will be a stronger competitor; the deal follows a bidding contest with Netflix and lawsuits brought by about a dozen US states.

segments.title: What changes for audiences and workers
segments.body: The merger’s settlement with US states requires at least 30 film releases a year for the first two years, rising to 32 for the next three, including independent films. Analysts expect streaming prices could rise over time, while a study cited by the BBC estimates the deal could cost about 4,500 film and television jobs in Los Angeles. Paramount disputes that analysis.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s consumer-focused report highlights obligations in the settlement but notes they expire after five years. It also reports concerns from entertainment workers and media advocates that the settlement does not prevent layoffs or guarantee newsroom independence.

content.headline: Children risk sniper fire on the way to school in Yemen’s Taiz
content.shortHeadline: Yemen’s children brave sniper fire to reach school
content.standfirst: Students in Taiz cross a dangerous front line to attend class as fighting intensifies. A mortar strike killed a three-year-old boy and left another child critically ill, according to BBC reporting from the city.

image.caption: Yemeni schoolgirls describe the danger of travelling to class near the front line.

sources.originalTitle: Children brave snipers and mortars to go to school near Yemen front line

segments.body: Ten-year-old Rafeef walks uphill to school in Taiz with her back to Houthi sniper positions, which lie across a contested valley. She says she is afraid, but does not want to stop going: school is one of her few chances to see friends, and she hopes to become a doctor. Her teacher says the school has been fired on before.

segments.title: Civilians caught in the fighting
segments.body: The BBC reports that the conflict has intensified around Taiz, with a vital supply route to Aden cut off on Sunday and residents fearing the Houthis could seize the city. At a nearby hospital, a three-year-old boy was killed by shrapnel from a mortar strike; an 11-year-old boy injured in the same incident remained critically ill after surgery.

content.headline: Quebec separatists projected to form minority government
content.shortHeadline: Quebec separatists projected to win minority government
content.standfirst: The Parti Québécois is projected to return to power for the first time since 2014, but its 28% share of the vote leaves it short of a majority and complicates its pledge to hold an independence referendum.

image.caption: Parti Québécois leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is projected to become Quebec’s premier.

sources.originalTitle: Separatist party projected to win Quebec election, adding new test to Canada's unity

segments.body: The Parti Québécois is projected to win enough seats to form a minority government in Quebec, with leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon set to become premier. The separatist party will need support from rivals to advance its plans, including a referendum on independence. Polls cited by the BBC indicate about 30% of Quebecers currently support separation.

segments.title: A test for Ottawa
segments.body: The PQ received 28% of the popular vote and is projected to fall short of the 64 seats needed for a majority. The Liberals say they will work with the party on some issues but oppose a referendum. Plamondon has also said he will challenge Ottawa on immigration and seek to end the monarchy’s role in Quebec, moves that could face legal obstacles.

content.headline: Far-right AfD wins speaker role in German state parliament
content.shortHeadline: AfD takes German state parliament speaker role
content.standfirst: Tobias Rausch’s election in Saxony-Anhalt marks a postwar first for a far-right party. The vote also exposes cracks in the convention that other parties should keep the AfD out of power.

image.caption: AfD politicians Ulrich Siegmund and Tobias Rausch after Rausch’s election as parliament speaker.

sources.originalTitle: State parliament elects Germany’s first far-right speaker since second world war

segments.body: Tobias Rausch of the Alternative für Deutschland was elected speaker of Saxony-Anhalt’s state parliament, winning 48 of 82 votes. The AfD holds 39 seats and lacks a majority; the result means at least nine other lawmakers backed him. The Guardian reports this is the first time since the second world war that a far-right party has secured a regional parliament’s speakership in Germany.

segments.title: The firewall under pressure
segments.body: Five members of the leftwing BSW had said they would vote for Rausch, arguing that the AfD’s support cannot be ignored. Their position challenges the political “firewall” by which other parties have shunned cooperation with the AfD. The party, which won nearly 44% in last month’s state election, is seeking to form a government by December.

content.headline: Uncertainty remains after Russian plague institute worker’s death
content.shortHeadline: Questions remain over death at Russian plague institute
content.standfirst: Russian authorities say a laboratory worker died of pneumonia of unknown cause and deny a plague case in Irkutsk. Experts say the risk appears limited, but the circumstances of her death have not been established.

image.caption: The anti-plague research institute in Irkutsk where the worker was employed.

sources.originalTitle: Rubio urges Russia to share more information on plague lab worker's death
What do we know about death of anti-plague institute worker in Russia and is there a wider risk?
Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague. This is what you should know
What is pneumonic plague and how does it spread?

segments.body: Darya Shipilova, 28, died on 2 October, two days after reportedly becoming unwell while working at an anti-plague institute in Irkutsk. Russia’s health watchdog says she died of “pneumonia of unknown aetiology” and told the World Health Organization that no plague case had been recorded in the city. Reports about a test-tube accident or exposure elsewhere remain unconfirmed.

segments.title: What is known about the risk
segments.body: Russian authorities say contacts have been identified and are being monitored; they have reported no symptoms among them. The WHO’s initial assessment, as quoted by the Guardian, rates the risk as moderate to low for Irkutsk, low for Russia and very low for the WHO European region. Experts say pneumonic plague can spread through close contact but is treatable with antibiotics when caught early.

perspectives.body: Experts cited by the Guardian emphasise that the case’s cause and any exposure route remain unclear. They call for transparency, while noting that monitoring contacts is sensible and the WHO’s initial assessment puts the wider regional risk very low.

content.headline: IceCube observatory pioneer Francis Halzen wins physics Nobel
content.shortHeadline: IceCube pioneer Francis Halzen wins physics Nobel
content.standfirst: The Belgian-born physicist is recognised for leading the South Pole observatory that detects high-energy neutrinos, giving scientists a new way to investigate violent processes across the universe.

image.caption: Francis Halzen, recognised for his work developing the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.

sources.originalTitle: 'Ghost particles' from space telescope wins physics Nobel

segments.body: Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his scientific leadership in developing IceCube, a neutrino observatory embedded in a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice. Thousands of sensors detect rare flashes produced when neutrinos interact with the ice, helping researchers trace the particles’ origins in distant, high-energy cosmic events.

segments.title: A new window on the universe
segments.body: Neutrinos can pass through dense matter and are not deflected by magnetic fields, so their paths can point back to distant sources that ordinary telescopes cannot readily observe. Halzen first proposed building a detector at the South Pole in 1988. He told a news conference he had been surprised that the idea worked so well.

content.headline: Trump’s remarks about attacks on California cities draw backlash
content.shortHeadline: Trump’s remarks about attacks on California cities draw fire
content.standfirst: California leaders condemned the president’s comments about Iran being able to “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego. The White House says he was warning of the danger of a nuclear-armed Iran.

image.caption: Donald Trump speaks about Iran at a campaign rally.

sources.originalTitle: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego

segments.body: Donald Trump said at a rally that Iran could “take out Los Angeles” or San Diego, adding that this would be “a small price to pay” for keeping the country safe. California Governor Gavin Newsom called the remarks “deranged and dangerous”; the mayors of Los Angeles and San Diego also criticised them.

segments.title: White House response
segments.body: White House communications director Stephen Cheung said Trump was describing how US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran had not been stopped. The White House also attacked news coverage of the comments. Trump has not responded to California leaders’ statements, the BBC reports.

content.headline: Seventh arrest in investigation near RAF Fairford; no charges filed
content.shortHeadline: Seventh arrest in RAF Fairford investigation; no charges
content.standfirst: A 22-year-old British man has been arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts after an incident near the Gloucestershire airbase. Six earlier arrests have been made, but nobody has been charged.

image.caption: A police roadblock outside RAF Fairford.

sources.originalTitle: British national arrested in connection with RAF Fairford incident
British man arrested over suspected RAF Fairford terrorism plot

segments.body: Counter-terrorism police arrested the man in Westminster on Tuesday as part of an investigation into events near RAF Fairford on 27 September. Five men were arrested at the scene and a sixth man was detained in Westminster later; all six were released on bail. Police say the investigation remains live and no one has been charged.

segments.title: Questions about the base
segments.body: The US has moved bombers away from Fairford after President Donald Trump said there had been threats, but gave no details. US media reports have suggested intelligence pointed to a possible Iranian drone attack; the BBC says it has not verified those reports. Iran’s embassy has denied involvement, according to the Guardian.

content.headline: Drax datacentre could emit more CO₂ than all Gatwick flights
content.shortHeadline: Drax datacentre could out-emit Gatwick flights, analysis says
content.standfirst: An environmental group estimates the proposed North Yorkshire facility could produce 8.6m tonnes of CO₂ a year if powered as planned by burning wood. Drax disputes the analysis and its assumptions.

image.caption: Drax power station in North Yorkshire, which burns imported wood for energy.

sources.originalTitle: Drax datacentre could create nearly twice the yearly emissions of all Gatwick flights

segments.body: Drax’s proposed 1.2GW datacentre at its North Yorkshire power station could require 4.9 million tonnes of wood a year, according to an estimate by the Natural Resources Defense Council based on Drax’s annual report. The group calculates emissions of 8.6 million tonnes of CO₂ annually—nearly twice the total from flights out of Gatwick in 2024—assuming continuous operation.

segments.title: Disputed climate claims
segments.body: Drax says the campaign group’s claims are inaccurate and not independently verified, disputing its assumptions about biomass accounting and the facility’s power mix. The planning process has not begun; the company says the project could be operational from 2031 if it receives consent. Campaigners are calling for stricter national standards for datacentre energy and emissions.

perspectives.body: Drax says the estimates do not reflect international greenhouse-gas accounting standards for biomass or the proposed power mix. Environmental campaigners counter that burning wood for server farms would be highly polluting and want the government to set clear limits.

content.headline: Nurseries expected to restrict staff phones and children’s photos
content.shortHeadline: Nursery staff face phone curbs under planned safeguarding rules
content.standfirst: New guidance is expected to limit personal devices in childcare areas and restrict routine photos of children, following abuse and data-security cases. The Department for Education says it is developing sector guidance.

image.caption: Planned guidance would restrict device use and photography in childcare settings.

sources.originalTitle: Nursery staff to be banned from using phones after ‘chilling’ child abuse case

segments.body: The government is expected to tell nursery staff, childminders and visitors not to use personal phones and devices in childcare areas. Staff would use a designated work device, with photos limited to one per child per day in routine circumstances, and parents would need to give written permission for images to be taken and shared.

segments.title: Safeguarding and implementation
segments.body: The proposed guidance follows the case of Vincent Chan, a nursery worker jailed for abusing children, and a cyberattack targeting a nursery chain. It is also expected to call for checks of work devices and caution against uploading identifiable children’s images to AI tools. A union representative says staff shortages and inconsistent training could make the rules harder to put into practice.

content.headline: £100,000 childcare threshold leaves some parents worse off after a pay rise
content.shortHeadline: Childcare support cliff edge hits parents just above £100,000
content.standfirst: Parents in England can lose funded childcare hours and their personal tax allowance when adjusted income crosses £100,000. Kemi Badenoch has pledged to remove the childcare threshold, putting pressure on Labour to respond.

image.caption: Parents just above the £100,000 income threshold can lose funded childcare support.

sources.originalTitle: The high-earning parents who can’t afford their children

segments.body: The £100,000 income limit for funded childcare can leave a parent worse off if a small pay rise takes them just over the threshold. The limit also coincides with the loss of the personal tax allowance. The i Paper reports that about 2.06 million workers now earn more than £100,000, up from roughly 1.2 million in 2021–22.

segments.title: A policy dispute
segments.body: The Institute for Fiscal Studies has criticised the system, and the article argues that a tapered reduction could avoid the sharp cutoff. Badenoch has pledged to end the childcare “trap”; the report says the £100,000 threshold has not risen since it was introduced in 2017. The government’s wider decisions on who should receive support remain contested.

content.headline: Staff shortages threaten promised specialist support for SEND pupils
content.shortHeadline: Staff shortages put SEND specialists scheme at risk
content.standfirst: The £1.8bn Experts at Hand programme aims to bring specialists into mainstream schools, but councils and sector groups warn that vacancies could limit access. The Department for Education says rollout is phased over three years.

image.caption: Schools minister Georgia Gould has promoted the Experts at Hand scheme.

sources.originalTitle: SEND pupils’ extra support at risk with schools unable to access specialist staff

segments.body: The government’s Experts at Hand scheme is intended to improve mainstream schools’ access to educational psychologists, speech and language therapists, occupational therapists and specialist teachers. But at least 36 councils have raised concerns about recruiting or retaining staff, according to analysis cited by Schools Week.

segments.title: Capacity and delivery
segments.body: A sector thinktank estimated that around 1,400 additional full-time-equivalent educational psychologists were needed to address shortages in nearly 100 council areas. Speech and Language UK says it has not received firm plans from councils it works with. The Department for Education rejects the suggestion that rollout is stalling, saying areas began delivery last month and will expand over time.

perspectives.body: The Department for Education says this is a phased three-year programme, not a stalled rollout, and that councils need time to build the specialist workforce. Schools and councils warn that shortages could nevertheless leave families expecting support that is not yet available.

content.headline: Dispute over funding for teachers’ 3.5% pay award leaves schools uncertain
content.shortHeadline: Schools question funding for teachers’ 3.5% pay rise
content.standfirst: Education Secretary Lucy Powell said pension savings would help schools meet the pay award, but unions say those savings are already in budgets. The Treasury reportedly did not approve describing them as new funding.

image.caption: Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the Labour conference.

sources.originalTitle: School budgets set to be squeezed to pay for teacher pay rises

segments.body: The government says schools can meet teachers’ 3.5% pay award after lower employer contributions to the Local Government Pension Scheme improved their finances. Unions argue the savings were already built into school budgets and therefore are not extra money to cover the award.

segments.title: Conflicting accounts
segments.body: The i Paper reports that a senior Whitehall source said the Treasury had not agreed to the Department for Education’s presentation of the savings as new funding. The NASUWT says schools need clarity on what services may have to be cut; the department says the pay award remains unchanged and the revised pension costs strengthen schools’ ability to afford it.

content.headline: Tories propose £10bn ‘Britannia Shield’ missile defence plan
content.shortHeadline: Tories’ £10bn missile shield plan faces cost questions
content.standfirst: The Conservatives propose a network of radar, command systems and interceptors to protect key UK sites. Previous estimates cited in the reporting put a full system at £80bn or more.

image.caption: A Royal Navy Type 45 destroyer, one of the UK assets able to intercept missiles.

sources.originalTitle: Badenoch denies ‘British Iron Dome’ plan – after Tories use phrase in press release
Badenoch promises ‘Britannia shield’ iron dome missile system to protect UK

segments.body: The Conservatives say their proposed Britannia Shield would connect new radar, command systems and interceptor weapons to protect military bases, power stations and other critical infrastructure. They estimate a cost of £10bn over 10 years and say a basic system could be in place during their first term in government.

segments.title: Scale and cost disputed
segments.body: The reporting contrasts the proposal with estimates of at least £80bn for an entry-level system from former defence chief Richard Barrons and other experts. The Conservatives say they would fund the plan through higher defence spending and welfare reductions. Labour says it is investing £1bn in air defences; Kemi Badenoch separately disputed describing the plan as a direct copy of Israel’s Iron Dome.

perspectives.body: In a separate interview, Badenoch said Britannia Shield would be a UK-specific system, not a replica of Israel’s Iron Dome, despite a party release describing it as “in essence a British Iron Dome”. The report also records a dispute over whether its proposed budget is credible.

content.headline: FCA to review treatment of whistleblower who died in Thailand
content.shortHeadline: FCA review follows death of whistleblower Simon Andriesz
content.standfirst: MPs want an independent assessment of how the financial regulator handled Simon Andriesz’s complaints. His family says he took his own life; his allegations against his former employer were disputed.

image.caption: Simon Andriesz, a former BGC Partners employee who raised concerns with regulators.

sources.originalTitle: MPs call for investigation after Lutnick-Epstein whistleblower dies

segments.body: Simon Andriesz, a former employee of BGC Partners, died in Thailand last month. His family said he took his own life and there was no suggestion of foul play. Before his death he had complained to the Financial Conduct Authority, the FBI and others about alleged business links involving former BGC chief Howard Lutnick and Jeffrey Epstein, and alleged misconduct at BGC.

segments.title: Regulator’s handling under scrutiny
segments.body: Andriesz said he felt “thoroughly let down” by the FCA, which had previously told him there was insufficient evidence to conclude he had faced retaliation. BGC denies retaliating against him and denied the alleged misuse of commission funds. The FCA says board member Lea Paterson will review how it interacted with Andriesz and his whistleblowing allegations.

content.headline: CPR data breach exposed personal details of 8.8 million people
content.shortHeadline: Danish CPR breach exposed data on 8.8 million people
content.standfirst: Authorities say unauthorised access lasted about 10 days and was discovered after an unusually large bill for searches by a company with legitimate register access. Investigators do not yet know who was responsible or how the data may be used.

image.caption: Authorities brief reporters on the CPR data breach and ongoing investigation.

sources.originalTitle: Sådan blev CPR-databrud opdaget: 'Det er ret chokerende'
CPR-læk blev opdaget på grund af dyr faktura

segments.body: Unauthorised users accessed CPR information on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September, after misusing a small Danish company’s legitimate access to the register. Authorities say the breach was detected when the company received an unusually large bill for searches. Names and addresses were among the information accessed.

segments.title: Investigation and safeguards
segments.body: The National Special Crime Unit says it is too early to identify who was behind the access or what method was used; there are no suspects at present. Officials say they do not know what the data will be used for, and it is not yet clear whether anyone will need a new CPR number. Experts cited by DR criticised the apparent lack of systematic monitoring.

perspectives.body: The chair of Denmark’s Cybersecurity Council called it “quite shocking” that an employee handling billing, rather than a monitoring system, appears to have alerted authorities to the large data extraction.

content.headline: Henrik Frandsen elected speaker of Denmark’s parliament
content.shortHeadline: Henrik Frandsen elected speaker amid criticism
content.standfirst: The Moderates MP won the Folketing’s top role despite a late withdrawal of support from the Alternative party over his handling of a 2019 land deal while mayor of Tønder.

image.caption: Henrik Frandsen is elected speaker of the Folketing in Copenhagen.

sources.originalTitle: Folketinget vælger Henrik Frandsen som formand efter kritik

segments.body: Henrik Frandsen of the Moderates has been elected speaker of the Folketing, succeeding Venstre’s Søren Gade. The result followed a vote in parliament on Tuesday. Alternative withdrew its backing hours beforehand, citing Frandsen’s role in a 2019 decision concerning land connected to his former rural property.

segments.title: Questions over the appointment
segments.body: Frandsen had received compensation for placing 12.4 hectares under nature protection. In 2019, when he was mayor of Tønder, the municipality approved returning the land to agricultural use during a one-day process; the report says this may have increased the property’s value by up to one million kroner. His election is also unusual because the Moderates are the parliament’s sixth-largest party.

content.headline: MobilePay to become Vipps in Denmark from 12 January
content.shortHeadline: MobilePay name to change to Vipps in January
content.standfirst: The app’s name and logo will align with the Nordic service, but its functions, contacts and payment history are set to remain unchanged. A branding expert says the company is giving up a familiar name with considerable recognition.

image.caption: MobilePay’s familiar blue app icon is being replaced by a Vipps-style smiley.

sources.originalTitle: MobilePay ofrer 'et af Danmarks stærkeste hverdagsbrands': En helt vild øvelse
MobilePay skifter navn

segments.body: MobilePay will change its name to Vipps in Denmark on 12 January, after its logo begins changing in the app. The service says the app itself will work as before and users need not take any action. The company says the rebrand completes its effort to create a common Nordic identity after the merger with Norway’s Vipps.

segments.title: A recognised name is retired
segments.body: Nearly 4.7 million people in Denmark use MobilePay, and “mobilepaye” entered the Danish dictionary in 2014. Branding consultant Eva Svavars calls the change a major undertaking because the name has become part of everyday language, but says a shared Nordic brand could make cross-border payments easier.

perspectives.body: Branding consultant Eva Svavars says MobilePay is giving up substantial brand recognition, but argues that a common Nordic payment service may be worth the cost of teaching users a new name.

content.headline: Bornholm neighbours offered compensation over energy island works
content.shortHeadline: Bornholm energy project compensation draws residents’ criticism
content.standfirst: The government proposes payments of 100,000 to 200,000 kroner for homes within 300 metres of the land facility. A residents’ association says the proposed amounts and distance limit do not reflect the impact.

image.caption: An architectural rendering of the planned Energiø Bornholm land facility.

sources.originalTitle: Regeringen vil kompensere naboer til stort landanlæg

segments.body: The government proposes compensation for residents living within 300 metres of the Energiø Bornholm land facility, citing noise, effects on the landscape and concerns about the future transformers. The proposed payments are 200,000 kroner within 100 metres, 150,000 kroner at 101–200 metres and 100,000 kroner at 201–300 metres.

segments.title: Residents seek individual assessments
segments.body: Michael Ellerman, chair of the local residents’ association, welcomed having a proposal but said the amounts and 300-metre limit did not reflect the expected loss in property value. He argues affected properties should instead be assessed individually. The government also proposes a full-compensation purchase option for homes within 80 metres of specified power lines and substations.

content.headline: Invasive nutria hunted to protect Rømø’s sea defences
content.shortHeadline: Hunters search Rømø for invasive nutria threatening dikes
content.standfirst: The South American rodent has been spotted several times on the Wadden Sea island. Conservation and dike officials warn that its burrowing could weaken defences protecting residents from storms and flooding.

image.caption: A coordinator points out an area on Rømø where nutria have been seen.

sources.originalTitle: På vadehavsø jagter de invasiv gnaver: 'Den er en stor trussel'

segments.body: Regulated hunters are searching for a nutria on Rømø after it was spotted several times. The invasive rodent digs tunnels and burrows in banks and dikes, raising concern on an island where coastal earthworks protect homes from storms and water.

segments.title: Sightings increasing
segments.body: Seven nutria were recorded in Denmark this year, compared with two last year, according to figures cited by DR. The species originated in South America and was brought to Europe for fur farming. A Wadden Sea National Park biologist says numbers are increasing and argues that control is needed to prevent an established population.

content.headline: Motorring 3 to gain lanes as speed limit falls to 90km/h
content.shortHeadline: Copenhagen ring road to expand as speed limit falls
content.standfirst: Most of the 17-kilometre route will expand from three to four lanes in each direction, with noise-reducing asphalt and a lower speed limit. Work is due to begin in 2027.

image.caption: Plans widen the Motorring 3 and add noise-reducing asphalt.

sources.originalTitle: En af Danmarks mest trafikerede motorveje skal nu udvides

segments.body: The agreement will widen most of Motorring 3, west of Copenhagen, from three to four lanes in each direction, using the hard shoulder as an extra lane. The speed limit will fall from 110km/h to 90km/h, and noise-reducing asphalt is planned. Work is expected to start in 2027 and finish in 2029 or 2030.

segments.title: Noise remains a concern
segments.body: The road carries more than 145,000 vehicles a day. The Danish Road Directorate estimates the new asphalt could reduce noise by three to four decibels for around 40% of nearby homes. Gladsaxe’s mayor welcomed the noise measures but said further action would still be needed for residents who remain affected.

content.headline: Helsingør and Aalborg bid to become European Capital of Culture
content.shortHeadline: Helsingør and Aalborg bid for 2032 culture title
content.standfirst: The two Danish cities have submitted applications to compete for the 2032 European Capital of Culture title. An international jury will assess their bids in November before the Danish city is chosen by the end of 2027.

sources.originalTitle: To danske byer vil være Europæisk Kulturhovedstad i 2032

segments.body: Helsingør and Aalborg have both submitted applications to become European Capital of Culture in 2032. The cities will present their bids to an international jury in November, when a shortlist is expected. Denmark is to select its city by the end of 2027; a Bulgarian city will also hold the title in 2032.

content.headline: Skive criticised for choosing restaurant without collective agreement for royal-
content.shortHeadline: Skive royal visit choice criticised over restaurant agreement
content.standfirst: The municipality’s choice of venue for a royal visit has drawn criticism because the restaurant has no collective agreement. The mayor says the location was chosen for its proximity to a new waterfront facility.

image.caption: King Frederik and Queen Mary are due to visit Skive during its anniversary celebrations.

sources.originalTitle: Kongeparret er inviteret på restaurant uden overenskomst: Politiker kalder det forkert

segments.body: Skive has invited King Frederik and Queen Mary to a meal at a restaurant without a collective agreement during the town’s 700th-anniversary celebrations. A local SF councillor and the 3F union criticised the choice, saying the municipality should set an example on employment conditions.

segments.title: Council defends venue
segments.body: Mayor Alfred Brunsgaard says the restaurant was chosen because it is close to a waterfront bathing facility the royal couple will inaugurate. He says the municipality cannot require a restaurant to have a collective agreement and that the booking has already been made. The restaurant did not respond to DR’s request for comment.

content.headline: Greg Freeman turns small-town unease into a feverish rock record
content.shortHeadline: Greg Freeman’s feverish, uneasy rock
content.standfirst: On All Set the Bone, the Vermont songwriter’s sharp, densely packed lyrics meet restless arrangements and a darker sound. The result is a record that seems to tremble with the possibility of coming apart.

sources.originalTitle: All Set the Bone

segments.body: Greg Freeman writes as if every moment is an emergency. On All Set the Bone, his characters are isolated and angry, moving through economically strained towns and lives that feel close to collapse. His voice cracks and skids across the songs, giving their carefully composed rock a raw, unsettled edge.

segments.title: A town in the songs
segments.body: The album’s upstate New York settings give its disappointments a particular texture: poor service on the radio, familiar faces and places worn down by rent and neglected infrastructure. Freeman’s lines can be funny and startlingly vivid, while the music shifts through changing tempos and dynamics rather than settling into straightforward bar rock.

content.headline: Why the Afrobeats label can flatten Africa’s diverse pop music
content.shortHeadline: The limits of the Afrobeats label
content.standfirst: Artists across the continent have objected to a catch-all term that can obscure distinct sounds and traditions. The challenge, this essay argues, is to build the documentation and context that let emerging styles stand on their own.

image.caption: Tyla at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards in Los Angeles.

sources.originalTitle: The west has a blinkered view of African music – and it’s hurting the whole continent’s culture

segments.body: The Afrobeats label has helped market African music internationally, but its broad use can turn many different traditions and experiments into one category. South African artist Tyla has argued that she represents amapiano, while Tems, Burna Boy and other artists have also described their music in terms that resist the umbrella label.

segments.title: When a sound needs a name
segments.body: The essay traces how the term spread as a marketing shorthand, then asks what is lost when it becomes the default description for African pop. It points to banku music, azonto and other styles that might have developed fuller identities with more local and international documentation. The responsibility, contributors argue, lies with artists, media and industry as well as those marketing music abroad.

content.headline: Metallica’s Sphere residency makes spectacle part of the set
content.shortHeadline: Metallica bring rarities and spectacle to the Sphere
content.standfirst: The opening night of Life Burns Faster pairs a no-repeat set with the venue’s huge visual effects. The review finds the band’s playing still powerful, even as the immersive production sometimes competes for attention.

image.caption: Metallica performing at the Sphere in Las Vegas.

sources.originalTitle: Metallica review – metal titans on fine form in spectacular rarities-focused show

segments.body: Metallica opened their 24-show Las Vegas residency with a set built around the depth of their catalogue rather than a run of familiar hits. The no-repeat format gives the band room to move across eras, and the first night leaves out “Enter Sandman” while making space for songs including “The Call of Ktulu” and “The Day That Never Comes.”

segments.title: The band and the room
segments.body: The Sphere’s enormous images turn songs into scenes: a giant Cthulhu stalks through Las Vegas during “The Call of Ktulu,” while the walls become a graveyard for “Master of Puppets.” The review finds the effect sometimes overwhelming, but says the band’s tight playing and energy remain in focus. It also sees the set’s rarities as a way to avoid becoming a nostalgia act.

content.headline: Liz Harris finds something restorative in making music with Helen
content.shortHeadline: Liz Harris on Grouper, Helen and the pull of collaboration
content.standfirst: The solitary artist behind Grouper discusses her dream-pop trio Helen, a viral track uploaded by a fraudster and the risks of digital music platforms. Collaboration, she says, has brought a welcome sense of community.

image.caption: Liz Harris of Grouper and Helen.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris has often kept the music industry at a distance, making as Grouper music shaped by voice, guitar or piano and space. With Helen, her trio with Jed Bindeman and Scott Simmons, she finds a different pleasure: the company of friends and a brighter, more collective sound. Making the group’s new album, Linda’s Head, felt restorative during a period of medical difficulty.

segments.title: A viral song, and its cost
segments.body: Harris’s track “Poison Tree” attracted a huge audience after circulating on TikTok, but she learned that someone else had fraudulently registered and uploaded it. She and her label were able to stop the scam and recover what she was owed. The experience left her wary of platforms where, she says, fake tracks and royalty fraud demand time and effort from independent musicians.

content.headline: Tom Morello’s solo album turns protest into a family affair
content.shortHeadline: Tom Morello on protest, family and his solo album
content.standfirst: On his first full-length solo rock album, the Rage Against the Machine guitarist brings his activism to the fore and works with his teenage son. He also recalls how his mother taught him that ordinary people can change the world.

image.caption: Tom Morello speaking about his music and activism.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Morello on Rage Against the Machine fans turning against him

segments.body: Tom Morello describes Everyone Gets What They Want as a collection of anti-racist, anti-fascist songs and a response to a worldwide far-right turn. The album brings together his heavy-rock sound and collaborations including Serj Tankian, Kneecap and his 15-year-old son Roman, who co-wrote five tracks.

segments.title: A lesson from his mother
segments.body: Morello traces his political outlook to Mary Morello, who died in June aged 102. He recalls her explaining, when he was six, why the family would forgo grapes during a United Farm Workers boycott: they could help the farmworkers by making a small sacrifice. He says that belief in ordinary people’s ability to act runs through his songs.

content.headline: Olivia Dean turns pop’s language of love into an affirming show
content.shortHeadline: Olivia Dean makes love the heart of her live show
content.standfirst: Opening her Australia and New Zealand tour in Melbourne, Dean balances big-band spectacle with an earnest account of what love means. The review finds a performance that is both playful and quietly feminist.

image.caption: Olivia Dean, whose live show blends theatrical pop with reflections on love.

sources.originalTitle: Olivia Dean review – a powerful, affirming night with a pop star at the height of her powers

segments.body: Olivia Dean’s Melbourne show surrounds her rich voice with a nine-piece band, a horn section and a theatrical backdrop. But the spectacle serves a sincere idea: songs from The Art of Loving explore love as more than romance, including the need to give oneself the care and attention offered to others.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul reissue reveals an album still in motion
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul: a Beatles classic, heard in new ways
content.standfirst: A deluxe edition brings together alternate mixes, outtakes and recording histories, reopening questions about an album often treated as a fixed turning point. The review finds its greatest pleasure in hearing how many versions can coexist.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: The new Rubber Soul special edition assembles the UK and US albums, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes and studio material. Rather than confirming a single definitive version, the collection draws attention to the choices and revisions behind the Beatles’ 1965 record—and to the pressure of making it quickly for a Christmas release.

segments.title: A classic made by people
segments.body: The outtakes show songs taking shape through changes in tempo, arrangement and performance. They complicate the idea that Rubber Soul was an inevitable leap forward, presenting instead a group of young musicians working through possibilities. The review’s conclusion is that the album remains powerful partly because no one version can claim to be the only real one.

content.headline: How ? and the Mysterians made garage rock history with “96 Tears”
content.shortHeadline: The unlikely rise and afterlife of “96 Tears”
content.standfirst: A home-recorded single by a group of Mexican-American teenagers became a US No 1 in 1966, then found a second life as a garage-rock touchstone. Its story runs from a family garage to the influence of later punk and indie bands.

sources.originalTitle: 'A hypnotic effect that fills you with joy': The incredible story of 96 Tears, the US's unlikeliest one-hit wonder

segments.body: “96 Tears” began with an organ riff and lyrics about heartbreak, made by young musicians rehearsing in the Balderrama family garage in Michigan. Released by a small label with a limited pressing and local promotion, the rough-edged single spread through radio play before reaching the top of the US chart.

segments.title: A second life
segments.body: The group’s subsequent releases failed to match the hit, but “96 Tears” endured as an example of urgent, stripped-down regional rock. The article traces its rediscovery through garage-rock compilations and revivals, showing how a brief chart success became part of the musical groundwork later artists drew on.

content.headline: The Lost Children of Tuam tells a devastating story without easy closure
content.shortHeadline: The Lost Children of Tuam resists easy closure
content.standfirst: Monica Dolan plays Catherine Corless, whose local-history research uncovered the missing burial records of children who died at a mother and baby home in Ireland. The film’s restraint gives the survivors’ testimony room, but offers no comforting resolution.

image.caption: Monica Dolan as Catherine Corless in The Lost Children of Tuam.

sources.originalTitle: The Lost Children of Tuam review – deeply serious retelling of Ireland’s devastating tragedy

segments.body: The film follows amateur historian Catherine Corless as she investigates St Mary’s mother and baby home in Tuam, County Galway. Her research finds death certificates for nearly 800 children but no burial records. The account treats the deaths and the discovery of mass graves with a deliberate seriousness, avoiding additions that might turn the tragedy into spectacle.

segments.title: No neat ending
segments.body: Monica Dolan’s performance anchors a story shaped by kitchen-table research and testimony from survivors, some of whom describe abuse and neglect by nuns. The review emphasises that the film does not offer a triumphant conclusion or a sense of closure: its final note is the unresolved pain left by what happened.

content.headline: The London film festival’s standouts range from Hamlet to Mike Leigh
content.shortHeadline: Twelve films to look out for at the London film festival
content.standfirst: The selection includes Andrew Scott as the gravely ill actor Ian Charleson, a new Manchester-set film and what may be Mike Leigh’s final feature. The critic’s survey also takes in historical drama, social realism and a returned vampire.

image.caption: Andrew Scott as Ian Charleson in Elsinore.

sources.originalTitle: Hamlet’s goodbye, the last of Leigh, Birmingham blues and a vampire in Vienna: 12 great films at the London film festival

segments.body: Among the festival picks is a film about Ian Charleson’s Hamlet at the National Theatre, a role he took on while seriously ill with Aids. The line-up also includes Carol Morley’s story of a teenager drawn into Manchester’s music scene, a Birmingham drama about the choices facing people approaching their 30s, and Mike Leigh’s intergenerational portrait of two women working in social care.

segments.title: Different worlds, different scales
segments.body: The wider selection moves from a black-and-white portrait of Thomas Mann and his daughter to a school-trip drama set at Pompeii, a social satire from Boots Riley and a vampire story set in contemporary Vienna. The roundup offers a useful map of the festival’s range, from intimate character studies to stranger genre experiments.

content.headline: Club Kid finds warmth without sanitising queer New York nightlife
content.shortHeadline: Club Kid celebrates queer nightlife without sanitising it
content.standfirst: Jordan Firstman’s debut follows a club promoter who unexpectedly becomes a father. Its comedy and new family bonds never erase the messier sides of nightlife, making the film a spirited portrait of chosen and blood family.

image.caption: Jordan Firstman and Miss Benny in Club Kid.

sources.originalTitle: Club Kid review – Jordan Firstman’s heartfelt comedy is irresistible

segments.body: Peter, played by Firstman, has spent years running a New York club night and avoiding responsibility. When a former party acquaintance arrives with a 10-year-old boy she says is his son, he has to make room for a child in a life built around late nights. Their growing bond unfolds through music, record shopping and the city they explore together.

segments.title: A party with its rough edges
segments.body: The review praises the film’s warmth and comic energy but values most that it does not turn parenthood into a simple lesson against clubbing. It lets queer nightlife be chaotic and imperfect while showing why it can also feel magical: shared music, dancing and the intimacy of a night that carries on into morning.

content.headline: The Yellow Tie gives a son’s portrait of conductor Sergiu Celibidache
content.shortHeadline: The Yellow Tie portrays a conductor who rejected recordings
content.standfirst: John Malkovich plays Sergiu Celibidache in a biopic directed by the conductor’s son. The film’s devotion to its subject yields a sturdy, heartfelt portrait, though the review questions how much his rejection of recorded music proves.

image.caption: John Malkovich as Sergiu Celibidache in The Yellow Tie.

sources.originalTitle: The Yellow Tie review – John Malkovich gives major hauteur as legendary record-hating maestro

segments.body: The Yellow Tie follows Romanian conductor Sergiu Celibidache, whose belief that music must be experienced live led him to reject recording offers. The film traces his rise after the war, his appointment with the Berlin Philharmonic and his later musical travels through Europe and Latin America.

segments.title: A conviction, not a consensus
segments.body: Directed by his son, Serge Ioan Celebidachi, the biopic is described as a labour of love: earnest and carefully made, if sometimes stately. The review finds a lonely heroism in Celibidache’s position but notes that the film does not establish why his view of recording should prevail over that of equally principled musicians who embraced it.

content.headline: Sergiu Celibidache was a demanding father as well as a musical visionary
content.shortHeadline: A son remembers the uncompromising Sergiu Celibidache
content.standfirst: Writing about The Yellow Tie, his film about the conductor, Serge Ioan Celebidachi recalls a father who was loving and generous but exacting at home and in teaching. He also explains why recordings of Celibidache’s performances were made without his knowledge.

image.caption: Sergiu Celibidache conducting in the early 1980s.

sources.originalTitle: Celibidache was a musical visionary, an uncompromising perfectionist – and my father

segments.body: Serge Ioan Celebidachi remembers a father who could be attentive and warm yet demanded complete commitment from the people around him. Sergiu Celibidache’s perfectionism shaped his family life and his teaching, where his son recalls harsh criticism of students. He describes his father’s intentions as sincere, while leaving open whether his methods were justified.

segments.title: The recordings he would not allow
segments.body: Celibidache believed recorded performances misrepresented music, which he felt could only be experienced live. His son says he arranged for some orchestras to record concerts without the conductor’s knowledge, valuing the recordings as memories of performances. He now feels grateful that those documents exist, despite the secrecy involved.

content.headline: The Craft’s high-school witches still make a fearless 90s spectacle
content.shortHeadline: The Craft retains its 90s high-school-horror bite
content.standfirst: The 30th-anniversary re-release revisits a supernatural story of teenage pain, power and revenge. The review finds an energetic cult film that stands apart from the decade’s more familiar high-school comedies.

image.caption: The young witches of The Craft.

sources.originalTitle: The Craft review – cult high-school horror a reminder of the fearless 90s

segments.body: Andrew Fleming’s 1996 film follows Sarah, a troubled new student who joins a group of girls practising witchcraft. Their powers give them a way to retaliate against people who have hurt them, but the balance within the group soon turns into a struggle for control between Sarah and Nancy.

The review describes The Craft as the darker counterpart to high-school comedies such as Clueless, with a supernatural edge and an unselfconscious energy associated with 1990s filmmaking. Its treatment of teenage anxiety may feel different from today’s conversations, but the film’s confidence and striking horror imagery remain part of its appeal.

content.headline: James Dean’s vulnerability outlasts the myth of the rebel
content.shortHeadline: James Dean beyond the rebel image
content.standfirst: A look back at East of Eden finds more than the restless gestures that made Dean an icon. The performance’s emotional centre is a young man reaching for the approval of a father who keeps him at a distance.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: The account of East of Eden’s production captures James Dean’s unpredictable presence on set and Elia Kazan’s decision to draw on the actor’s strained relationship with his father. The resulting Cal is restless and difficult to read, but the performance also makes him someone audiences can feel compelled to follow.

segments.title: The image and the person
segments.body: Dean died aged 24 after completing three starring roles, and the circumstances of his death helped turn him into an enduring symbol of rebellion. The essay argues that his most affecting moment is quieter: Cal reaching out to his rejecting father, a gesture that cuts through the cool, carefully preserved image.

content.headline: Digger makes Tom Cruise’s oil tycoon a deliberately divisive spectacle
content.shortHeadline: Digger is Tom Cruise’s bold, divisive eco-satire
content.standfirst: Alejandro G Iñárritu’s film casts Cruise as a blustering oil baron facing a climate catastrophe. Its excesses and high-concept turns will not suit everyone, but the review finds a politically blunt, unexpectedly ambitious satire.

image.caption: Tom Cruise in prosthetic make-up as Digger Rockwell.

sources.originalTitle: Digger review: Tom Cruise takes the 'biggest risk of his career' in this 'love-it-or-hate-it' folly ★★★★☆

segments.body: Cruise transforms himself with prosthetics into Digger Rockwell, an oil billionaire whose company’s drilling triggers a glacier disaster. As an iceberg threatens cities, a crisis meeting gathers around him, while a scientist struggles to make the danger understood. The review sees the premise as an eco-satire that feels less far-fetched than it might have a few years ago.

segments.title: A risk by design
segments.body: The film’s broad performance, political bluntness and two major twists make it a love-it-or-hate-it proposition, not a conventional prestige vehicle. The reviewer admires Cruise’s commitment to the oddball scale of the role, while acknowledging that some scenes run long and the spectacle can become excessive.

content.headline: Damilola: The Untold Story remembers a child, not just a crime
content.shortHeadline: Damilola: The Untold Story puts friendship first
content.standfirst: John Boyega and other childhood friends recall the night Damilola Taylor was killed, alongside the caretaker who found him. The documentary resists true-crime spectacle to focus on grief, memory and a boy whose life began in a new community.

image.caption: Damilola Taylor, remembered by friends in the documentary.

sources.originalTitle: Damilola: The Untold Story review – John Boyega’s trauma after losing his childhood friend is haunting

segments.body: The documentary returns to the killing of 10-year-old Damilola Taylor in 2000 through people who knew him as a friend. John Boyega recalls being frightened by the death of a child; his sister Grace describes standing up for Damilola at school and the guilt she carried over not walking him home that night.

segments.title: A community’s memory
segments.body: Rather than relying on graphic reconstructions or profiling, the film uses archive footage and testimony from Damilola’s friends, the caretaker who found him and journalist Sandra Laville. It also presents North Peckham as a community, not a shorthand for deprivation, while acknowledging that the killing deepened fear and violence for young people who lived there.

content.headline: Pierre gives David Harewood a distinctive role in Black British crime drama
content.shortHeadline: David Harewood anchors the crime drama Pierre
content.standfirst: Harewood plays a night-shift police-station duty solicitor drawn into a case involving alleged police harassment. The review praises the show’s noir confidence and its focus on the compromises of being a Black professional working around the police.

image.caption: David Harewood as Pierre, a duty solicitor in the Channel 4 drama.

sources.originalTitle: Pierre review – David Harewood’s twisty noir is an instant crime classic

segments.body: In Pierre, David Harewood plays a duty solicitor rather than a police officer. The story begins when a young Black man is found dead after telling Pierre he was building a case against an officer. Harewood’s presence, the nocturnal setting and the show’s assured visual style give the crime drama its force.

segments.title: A wider jurisdiction
segments.body: The review sees Pierre’s work as a way to examine the daily indignities and trade-offs of operating around an institution with a history of racism, while remaining connected to his community. It also notes that the show sometimes compresses complicated questions into too little dialogue, even as it marks a significant step for Black British crime drama.

content.headline: Jaclyn Smith looks back on Charlie’s Angels, friendship and life on set
content.shortHeadline: Jaclyn Smith remembers Charlie’s Angels
content.standfirst: Fifty years after the crime series began, its only original Angel to stay through the final season recalls the show’s sisterhood, its pay negotiations and the pressures around fame. She also discusses harassment and drug use on set.

image.caption: Jaclyn Smith, the only original Charlie’s Angels lead to stay through the series’ final season.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We got that bad guy and took him down!’ Jaclyn Smith on the fun, friendship and frustration of Charlie’s Angels

segments.body: Jaclyn Smith remembers Charlie’s Angels as a workplace built around women pursuing criminals, even as its glamorous look invited criticism. She says the original cast became close friends, and describes standing firm when she was offered less than Farrah Fawcett despite doing comparable work.

segments.title: The pressures behind the glamour
segments.body: Smith also discusses stalking, sexual harassment and the cocaine use she saw during the later seasons. She says the show’s popularity brought intrusion as well as opportunity, and that she tried to keep working while staying apart from the excesses around her.

content.headline: The Reluctant Vampire turns Eric Morecambe’s books into a comic family treat
content.shortHeadline: The Reluctant Vampire is a gag-filled family comedy
content.standfirst: Lenny Rush leads an adaptation of Eric Morecambe’s children’s books about a human boy raised in a vampire family. The review praises its warm silliness, committed cast and jokes that work for adults as well as younger viewers.

image.caption: Lenny Rush as Valentine in The Reluctant Vampire.

sources.originalTitle: The Reluctant Vampire review – Lenny Rush’s absolute joy of a comedy is perfectly cast

segments.body: Valentine is the second son in a family of vampires, but he has no fangs, dislikes blood and cannot turn into a bat. He eventually learns he is human, rescued as a baby and raised by the family. Lenny Rush gives the boy’s awkward search for belonging a comic centre, with Tom Davis and Sian Clifford as his parents.

The review enjoys the series’ crowded cast of vampires, gargoyles and other creatures, as well as its steady stream of jokes. Adapted by the team behind Alan Partridge, it keeps the books’ warmth and daftness while aiming to entertain the whole family rather than relying on adult snark.

content.headline: Strictly’s Amy Dowden deserved a better chance to shine this year
content.shortHeadline: Amy Dowden deserved a better Strictly pairing
content.standfirst: The professional dancer’s early exit for a second year running prompts questions about the show’s pairings. The argument is that Strictly’s pros are central to its appeal—and Dowden’s resilience should not be the only story the programme gives her.

image.caption: Amy Dowden, whose early elimination prompted debate about Strictly’s pairings.

sources.originalTitle: Amy Dowden’s exit exposes one big Strictly problem

segments.body: Strictly Come Dancing’s partnerships are often the heart of the competition, but Amy Dowden has been eliminated in the first week for a second year running. The column argues that pairing her with a celebrity who struggled to dance left the professional with little opportunity to show her strengths as a teacher and performer.

segments.title: More than resilience
segments.body: Dowden has faced an injury, a difficult celebrity pairing and breast cancer treatment during her recent Strictly years. The writer says her return to the dancefloor has been deeply moving, but argues that she deserves a season defined by the partnership she builds—not only by her ability to endure hardship.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future puts a beloved television institution on pause
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ partnership, cancelled a planned Christmas special and has no announced new Doctor. Fans and former contributors disagree over what went wrong, but share a fear that the series may disappear from the screen for too long.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, from Christopher Eccleston to Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Since the 2025 series ended with Ncuti Gatwa’s departure, Doctor Who has been left without an announced lead actor or a confirmed next season. The BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+ and cancelled a Christmas special while seeking a new funding partner. The corporation has declined to discuss the production’s future in detail.

segments.title: What the show has meant
segments.body: Fans and contributors point to different possible causes, from scripts and casting to the end of the co-production deal; the article notes that there is no settled explanation. Its longer history offers a reminder that the show has survived a 16-year gap before, while supporters argue that its values of kindness and curiosity still give it room to return.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a new British Asian family to the legal-drama universe
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up adds a British Asian family to the drama
content.standfirst: The spin-off relocates the family-law firm drama to Manchester, with Ritu Arya and Sanjeev Bhaskar leading a predominantly British Asian cast. Its creative team says the aim is to portray a family living ordinary lives, while keeping the original show’s appetite for relationship turmoil.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: Ritu Arya stars as Aria Kishan, a barrister expected to take over her father’s firm, until a family death changes the succession plans. The six-part series keeps the original The Split’s mix of divorce cases and family conflict but moves the story to Manchester and centres a new British Asian family.

segments.title: Representation in everyday life
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted the characters to be a normal family rather than representatives placed in exceptional circumstances. The series also gives its women a larger role across writing, performance and production, an ambition executive producer Abi Morgan says is part of her work to build women-led ensembles.

content.headline: 70 Up ends a landmark experiment—and revisits its participants’ misgivings
content.shortHeadline: 70 Up closes its long-running portrait of a generation
content.standfirst: The final chapter of ITV’s series catches up with participants first filmed as children in 1964. As it reaches its conclusion, the programme also gives space to people who felt reduced or misrepresented by the camera.

image.caption: The participants at the beginning of the Up documentary series in 1964.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A little pill of poison’: Why the cast of 70 Up came to resent it

segments.body: Beginning as Seven Up!, the documentary series followed 14 children from different backgrounds and returned to them every seven years. Its final instalment finds the remaining participants reflecting on age, work and family, while revisiting some of the lives the programme has made familiar to viewers.

segments.title: The limits of a portrait
segments.body: The ending also considers the participants’ complicated relationship with the series. Peter Davies left for decades after his comments about education and politics drew tabloid attention; others felt the programme’s framing missed important parts of their lives. Producer Helen Houston argues that trust endured, while Davies says no short television account can contain a whole person.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day has thrilling combat but little else to sustain it
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day’s combat outpaces its story
content.standfirst: The prequel delivers the series’ strongest-feeling combat yet, with destructible environments and weighty weapons. But repetitive routes, cluttered levels and intrusive collectibles leave the reviewer disappointed by everything around the fighting.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day returns to the invasion that began the Gears of War saga, following Marcus Fenix and his squad as alien creatures emerge from beneath the ground. The opening offers flashes of the horror and grimness of the early games, while the combat feels more fluid and the environments break apart convincingly under fire.

segments.title: A promising premise stretched thin
segments.body: The review’s main complaint is that the game repeatedly sends players back through similar parts of the damaged city, with little variety to offset the repetition. Large areas fill with collectibles and side objectives, and the chimes can disrupt story moments. The result is a game whose excellent cover-based combat is let down by what surrounds it.

content.headline: Resident Evil film recreates the fear and scarcity of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: Resident Evil captures the games’ survival-horror feel
content.standfirst: Zach Cregger’s adaptation leaves familiar heroes and locations aside to focus on a vulnerable courier trapped in an outbreak. Its attention to exploration, scarce ammunition and unsettling encounters makes the case for a different kind of game-to-film translation.

image.caption: Zach Cregger and actor Austin Abrams on the Resident Evil film set.

sources.originalTitle: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations

segments.body: The film centres on Bryan Hodukavich, a courier caught in a viral outbreak with no weapon and little understanding of what is happening. As he moves through a farmhouse, tunnel, hospital and sewer, he finds stronger weapons but remains short on ammunition, echoing the practical pressures of the games.

segments.title: A player’s point of view
segments.body: Rather than reproducing the familiar heroes, the adaptation tries to recreate the uncertainty of playing: piecing together events through recordings and brief exchanges, and never knowing whether the protagonist will survive. The article connects this approach to the vulnerability of the series’ characters and to films that examine how video games make audiences participants as well as spectators.

content.headline: Ace Combat 8 turns aerial dogfights into a compelling Top Gun fantasy
content.shortHeadline: Ace Combat 8 makes aerial combat soar
content.standfirst: The latest entry pairs accessible, spectacular dogfights with a more emotionally ambitious story. Its missions deliver tension and visual drama, though the cockpit can become cluttered and the dialogue occasionally strains for effect.

image.caption: A fighter jet in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.

sources.originalTitle: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy

segments.body: Ace Combat 8 puts players in the role of a fictional ace pilot whose legend begins as wartime propaganda. The arcade-style flying prioritises exhilaration over realism, with approachable controls for newcomers and more demanding manoeuvres for veterans. The review finds the dogfights thrilling and the skies exceptionally beautiful.

segments.title: More than a dogfight
segments.body: Missions range from bombing runs to hunting invisible aircraft, while new cinematic sequences give squadmates and their stories more presence than in the previous game. The reviewer finds some objectives hard to read amid the action and some dialogue clunky, but says the narrative and presentation land with unexpected emotional force.

content.headline: Roblox phishing scams target children with fake free-Robux offers
content.shortHeadline: How fake Robux offers target young Roblox players
content.standfirst: Fraudsters use convincing imitation sign-in pages to steal account details, in-game currency and personal data. Parents can reduce the risk by encouraging children to open Roblox directly and never share authentication codes.

image.caption: Roblox users are advised to avoid unknown links and use the official app or website.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting children

segments.body: The scam begins with a promise of free Robux, often in a comment or chat on platforms such as YouTube, TikTok or Discord. A link leads to a fake Roblox login page; after a child enters their details, it redirects them to the real service, making the theft less obvious.

segments.title: How to lower the risk
segments.body: Cybersecurity experts quoted in the report advise opening the game through its official app or website rather than links sent by others. Two-factor authentication remains useful, but its codes and backup codes should be treated like passwords. Roblox warns it cannot guarantee recovery of lost currency or virtual items.

content.headline: Playing Modern Warfare 2 with his adult son brings a father back to gaming
content.shortHeadline: A father and son reconnect through an old game
content.standfirst: Replaying the co-op missions they first tried when his son was five, a father discovers that teamwork—and time together—has improved. Their gaming sessions become a joyful way to revisit an old bond before they move to different parts of the world.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game the writer revisits with his son.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The writer and his 22-year-old son return to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the first game they played together. Once difficult co-op missions become shared challenges again: the son learns to hold back, his father becomes less cautious, and they finally defeat the guard dogs that used to end their attempts.

segments.title: A brief return to gaming time
segments.body: Their sessions bring back the freedom of playing for hours without the responsibilities that can crowd out a hobby. The writer knows the arrangement is temporary, as they will soon move to different parts of the world, but his son says he will remember these weeks as some of their best times together.

content.headline: The White House’s arcade games show how play can be weaponised
content.shortHeadline: The White House turns game imagery into propaganda
content.standfirst: A collection of government-hosted mini-games borrows familiar formats to mock migrants and promote political messaging. The column argues that their crude execution should not obscure the wider reach of gaming aesthetics in political communication.

image.caption: A screenshot from Build the Wall, one of the White House arcade games.

sources.originalTitle: The Trump White House’s fetish for gamer culture has moved up a level with new arcade

segments.body: The White House arcade repurposes familiar game styles in exercises including Build the Wall and Rio Run. The columnist describes the games as crude propaganda, with migrants turned into targets or obstacles, and argues that the playful graphics do not soften their dehumanising premise.

segments.title: A medium with political reach
segments.body: The article places the arcade in a longer effort to borrow gaming imagery for political messaging, while distinguishing this from artists and activists using games to express political ideas. It cautions that the mini-games may be designed more to provoke than persuade, but says the medium’s potential to reach and influence audiences should not be dismissed.

content.headline: Pokémon’s volunteer professors keep competitive play running
content.shortHeadline: The volunteers behind competitive Pokémon
content.standfirst: At the 2026 world championships, volunteer Pokémon professors judged matches, helped players and managed the event floor. Their work includes difficult rulings and practical support, while how they are compensated remains unclear.

image.caption: Competitors and attendees at the 2026 Pokémon World Championships in San Francisco.

sources.originalTitle: Meet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling

segments.body: The Pokémon Professor Program supplies volunteers who help run official events around the world. At the San Francisco championships, their jobs ranged from refereeing and explaining rules to checking results and keeping the venue safe. One head judge described the work as a mix of tournament administration and dealing with players under pressure.

segments.title: Rules and relationships
segments.body: Professors say their role is not only to make calls but to help competitors enjoy the game and understand decisions. The report also notes that the company declined to explain its compensation arrangements; volunteers described different support, including merchandise, wages at some events and travel assistance.

content.headline: GTA VI’s virtual romance prompts a real debate about relationship boundaries
content.shortHeadline: Does GTA VI’s romance cross a relationship line?
content.standfirst: Online debate has focused on players maintaining the bond between protagonists Lucia and Jason. The article rejects a universal rule about virtual romance, while taking seriously the insecurity some partners describe when game relationships seem to meet needs missing offline.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason, the central couple in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

segments.body: In the reported design of Grand Theft Auto VI, players can strengthen the relationship between Lucia and Jason through dates, messages and other interactions. Some social media users have called this kind of play unfaithful, prompting a wider argument about whether virtual romance can cross a real relationship’s boundaries.

segments.title: The argument beneath the joke
segments.body: The writer considers it unreasonable to treat every in-game romance as cheating, while noting that boundaries differ between couples. They argue that some responses reveal a more serious worry: that a partner may invest attention in a fictional relationship while neglecting a real one. The debate, the article suggests, speaks to loneliness and disconnection as much as to games.

content.headline: Nobel prize honours Francis Halzen and IceCube’s neutrino astronomy
content.shortHeadline: Nobel honours IceCube neutrino astronomy
content.standfirst: Francis Halzen helped turn Antarctic ice into a detector for elusive particles arriving from space. The prize recognises work that opened a new way to study the universe, beyond light and gravitational waves.

image.caption: The IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station in Antarctica.

sources.originalTitle: Nobel prize in physics goes to Francis Halzen for south pole work on neutrinos

segments.body: The 2026 Nobel prize in physics has been awarded to Francis Halzen, a Belgian physicist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, for decisive contributions to the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin. The prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor.

segments.title: A new way to observe the cosmos
segments.body: IceCube uses thousands of light detectors embedded in a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice to pick up faint flashes from neutrinos colliding with atomic nuclei. Its first detection of high-energy neutrinos from outside our solar system came in 2013; researchers later identified a cosmic source billions of light-years away. The observations have helped establish neutrinos as another messenger for studying the universe.

content.headline: Nobel prize recognises discoveries that made brain cells light-sensitive
content.shortHeadline: Nobel honours optogenetics and brain research
content.standfirst: Work on light-gated ion channels led to optogenetics, a technique that lets researchers control nerve cells with light. The method has transformed studies of brain circuits and is also being explored in treatment.

image.caption: The three Nobel laureates, Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, shown during the prize announcement.

sources.originalTitle: Nobel prize in medicine 2026 awarded for research into mysteries of brain

segments.body: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have won the 2026 Nobel prize in physiology or medicine for discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. Their work enabled scientists to use light-sensitive proteins to switch nerve cells on or off, making it possible to investigate how particular brain circuits function.

segments.title: From algae to brain circuits
segments.body: The research began with Hegemann’s study of how green algae respond to light. Hegemann and Nagel identified channelrhodopsins, proteins that let charged particles flow through cells when exposed to light. Deisseroth and colleagues later used the proteins in nerve cells in animals, allowing researchers to test how activity in particular cells relates to movement, memory and behaviour.

segments.title: A route towards treatment
segments.body: Optogenetics has also informed early therapeutic work. In one trial, researchers used a channelrhodopsin gene and light-stimulating goggles to partially restore sight in a man with retinitis pigmentosa. The result is an example of an experimental application, not evidence that the approach is an established treatment for blindness.
